blocks.text:
Design an ad click aggregator, the system that ingests a massive stream of ad click and impression events and turns them into per-ad counts, powering both near real time advertiser dashboards and, far more critically, the exact figures advertisers are actually billed against. This category's three prior problems all counted or ranked things where an occasional approximation was an acceptable, even deliberate, trade-off. This one cannot make that same trade for its most important output, since a miscounted click is not a cosmetic inaccuracy, it is real money charged incorrectly to a real advertiser.

The two techniques that make this possible are event-time windowed aggregation with watermarks, which decide when a time window can safely be considered done, and a two-layer lambda-style architecture, a fast streaming layer for dashboards paired with a slower, exact batch layer that reprocesses the full raw log for billing.

This one cannot make that same trade for its most important output, since a miscounted click is not a cosmetic inaccuracy, it is real money charged incorrectly to a real advertiser.

The two techniques that make this possible are event-time windowed aggregation with watermarks, which decide when a time window can safely be considered done, and a two-layer lambda-style architecture, a fast streaming layer for dashboards paired with a slower, exact batch layer that reprocesses the full raw log for billing.

blocks.text: The system should ingest click and impression events at high volume and aggregate them into per-ad, per-time-window counts. Advertisers should see a near real time dashboard of their ad's performance. The platform should produce exact, final counts per ad per billing period, used for actual invoicing. Events that arrive late, after their window has already been considered closed, should still be correctly incorporated into the final billing figures rather than silently lost. Fraudulent or invalid clicks should be identified and excluded before they ever reach a bill.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter here, and the very first one is what separates this design from every other counting system in this category.

blocks.alt: Exact counting for billing, low latency dashboards, scalable ingestion, fraud resistance, and durable, no lost events

blocks.text: Exact counting for billing means the final numbers this system produces are not an estimate, advertisers are charged based on them directly, so an undercount or an overcount is a genuine financial error, not a rounding nuance. Low latency dashboards means advertisers still expect to see roughly current performance within seconds, even though the exact billing figures are allowed to finalize more slowly. Scalable ingestion means the system has to absorb millions of events per second across the whole ad platform. Fraud resistance means a bot, or a competitor deliberately clicking an ad to drain its budget, must not generate real charges. And durability means a dropped event is not a recoverable bug, it is a permanent, uncorrectable loss of real revenue for either the advertiser or the platform.

blocks.text: This design assumes the event ingestion pipeline delivers at-least-once, meaning a network retry can redeliver the same event more than once, and deduplication by a unique event id is required to avoid double counting, covered in section 7. Windows are defined by event time, when the click actually happened, not by when it happened to arrive at the server. A bounded allowed lateness controls how long a window stays open for straggling events before the streaming layer considers it closed, while the batch layer's reconciliation pass is what actually finalizes the exact billing number, incorporating any event that arrived even later than that.

blocks.text: At real platform scale, click and impression events can arrive at a combined rate of millions per second, spread across tens of millions of distinct active ads. Only a small fraction of events genuinely arrive late, after their window's watermark has passed, but that fraction still has to be handled correctly rather than dropped, since each one represents real, billable activity. Dashboards can afford to lag live activity by a few seconds; the exact, final billing figures are allowed to lag considerably further, precisely so they have time to absorb whatever arrives late.

blocks.text: An incoming click or impression event is durably logged in full and simultaneously pushed onto a streaming ingest queue. On the streaming side, a fraud filter screens it, a deduplicator rejects it if its event id has already been counted, and a windowed aggregator groups it by ad and event-time window, publishing near real time counts to a dashboard store. Separately and on a slower cadence, a batch reconciliation job reprocesses the complete raw event log, including anything that arrived too late for the streaming layer's windows, and publishes the exact, final counts that billing actually relies on.

blocks.text: The happy path is the ingest flow above, a fresh, on-time, genuine event flows straight through into both the near real time dashboard and, eventually, the exact billing figure with no correction needed. The workflow worth walking through separately is a late event, one whose window the streaming layer already considered closed by the time it arrives. Rather than being dropped, it lands in the late-event store, and the next scheduled batch reconciliation pass folds it into that window's count before that window is ever marked finalized for billing, so the exact figure advertisers are actually charged against is always correct, even though the earlier, near real time dashboard figure briefly undercounted it.

from typing import Dict, List, Set


# One click event, carrying the identity needed for both deduplication and windowing.
class ClickEvent:
    def __init__(self, event_id: str, ad_id: str, event_time_millis: int):
        self.event_id = event_id            # unique id, used to detect retried duplicates
        self.ad_id = ad_id                     # which ad this click belongs to
        self.event_time_millis = event_time_millis   # when the click actually happened, not when it arrived


# Groups events into fixed-size event-time windows per ad, deduplicates by event
# id, and routes events that arrive after their window's watermark has passed
# into a separate late-event store instead of silently dropping them.
class WindowedAggregator:
    def __init__(self, window_size_millis: int):
        self._window_size_millis = window_size_millis                         # size of each aggregation window
        self._seen_event_ids: Set[str] = set()                                   # every event id counted so far, for dedup
        self._counts_by_ad_and_window: Dict[str, Dict[int, int]] = {}                # adId -> windowStart -> count
        self._late_events: List[ClickEvent] = []                                        # events that missed their window
        self._watermark = 0                                                                # how far event time has progressed

    # Returns true if this event was late (routed to the late store), false if it
    # was processed normally (either counted, or rejected as a duplicate).
    def process(self, event: ClickEvent) -> bool:
        if event.event_id in self._seen_event_ids:
            return False   # a duplicate, at-least-once retry; never counted twice

        window_start = self._window_start_for(event.event_time_millis)   # which window this event's time falls into
        window_end = window_start + self._window_size_millis

        if window_end <= self._watermark:
            # This event's window has already closed from the streaming layer's point of
            # view, so it is stored separately instead of silently being dropped.
            self._late_events.append(event)
            return True

        self._seen_event_ids.add(event.event_id)   # mark this event id as counted, guarding against future duplicates
        windows = self._counts_by_ad_and_window.setdefault(event.ad_id, {})   # get or create this ad's window map
        windows[window_start] = windows.get(window_start, 0) + 1                 # increment this window's count by 1
        return False

    # Advances the watermark, closing any window that now ends at or before it.
    def advance_watermark(self, new_watermark: int) -> None:
        self._watermark = new_watermark

    def get_count(self, ad_id: str, window_start: int) -> int:
        windows = self._counts_by_ad_and_window.get(ad_id)
        if windows is None:
            return 0
        return windows.get(window_start, 0)

    # Folds a previously-late event directly into its correct window's count,
    # called only by the reconciliation job, bypassing the watermark check since
    # reconciliation runs after all lateness has already been accounted for.
    def reconcile_late_event(self, event: ClickEvent) -> None:
        if event.event_id in self._seen_event_ids:
            return   # still guard against double counting even during reconciliation
        self._seen_event_ids.add(event.event_id)
        window_start = self._window_start_for(event.event_time_millis)
        windows = self._counts_by_ad_and_window.setdefault(event.ad_id, {})
        windows[window_start] = windows.get(window_start, 0) + 1

    def drain_late_events(self) -> List[ClickEvent]:
        drained = list(self._late_events)
        self._late_events.clear()
        return drained

    def _window_start_for(self, event_time_millis: int) -> int:
        return (event_time_millis // self._window_size_millis) * self._window_size_millis   # floor to the start of this event's window


# Periodically reprocesses every stored late event, correcting the aggregator's
# counts so the final, exact figures used for billing include everything.
class ReconciliationJob:
    def __init__(self, aggregator: WindowedAggregator):
        self._aggregator = aggregator

    def run(self) -> None:
        for late_event in self._aggregator.drain_late_events():
            self._aggregator.reconcile_late_event(late_event)   # fold each late event into its correct window's exact count


if __name__ == "__main__":
    window_size_millis = 60000   # each window covers 1 minute of event time

    aggregator = WindowedAggregator(window_size_millis)

    # Two genuine events for ad-1, both inside the window [0, 60000).
    aggregator.process(ClickEvent("evt-1", "ad-1", 1000))
    aggregator.process(ClickEvent("evt-2", "ad-1", 2000))

    # A duplicate delivery of evt-1, simulating an at-least-once retry.
    aggregator.process(ClickEvent("evt-1", "ad-1", 1000))

    # One genuine event for a different ad, ad-2, same window.
    aggregator.process(ClickEvent("evt-3", "ad-2", 1500))

    # Advance the watermark past this window's end, closing it for the streaming layer.
    aggregator.advance_watermark(60000)

    print("Before reconciliation:")
    print(f"  ad-1 window [0,60000) count: {aggregator.get_count('ad-1', 0)}")
    print(f"  ad-2 window [0,60000) count: {aggregator.get_count('ad-2', 0)}")
    print(f"  duplicate evt-1 correctly not double counted: {str(aggregator.get_count('ad-1', 0) == 2).lower()}")

    # A late event for ad-1, event time 500, belongs to the already-closed window [0,60000).
    late_event = ClickEvent("evt-4", "ad-1", 500)
    was_late = aggregator.process(late_event)
    print(f"Late event correctly routed to the late store instead of the live window: {str(was_late).lower()}")
    print(f"  ad-1 window [0,60000) count still unchanged before reconciliation: {aggregator.get_count('ad-1', 0)}")

    # The batch reconciliation job picks up every stored late event and folds it in.
    reconciliation = ReconciliationJob(aggregator)
    reconciliation.run()

    print("After reconciliation:")
    print(f"  ad-1 window [0,60000) exact final count: {aggregator.get_count('ad-1', 0)}")
    print(f"  ad-2 window [0,60000) exact final count: {aggregator.get_count('ad-2', 0)}")

items: Architecture: a fast streaming layer with fraud filtering, deduplication, and event-time windowed aggregation for dashboards, paired with a slower batch reconciliation layer that reprocesses the full raw log into exact billing figures.
Capacity: millions of click and impression events per second across tens of millions of active ads, with a deliberate gap between near real time dashboard lag and slower, exact billing lag.
The core techniques: deduplication by event id, event-time windowing with watermarks, and late-event reconciliation, all worked through with a real, verified implementation.
Database: an append-only raw event log as the source of truth, with a separate, read-optimized dashboard store for near real time figures.
End-to-end workflows: a normal ingest-and-aggregate flow and a late-event reconciliation flow, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: eventually consistent, near real time dashboard counts versus strongly consistent, exact billing counts, finalized only after reconciliation.
Trade-offs: streaming-only versus a lambda-style streaming-plus-batch architecture versus batch-only, compared directly on speed, exactness, and where each breaks down.
